Pakistan reaches $1.2 billion IMF deal to manage economic inflation and West Asia conflict fallout

The deal would give Pakistan about $1 billion under its main lending program and another $210 million under a separate climate fund.

Bilal Hussain

08 October, 2026 02:08 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

The IMF headquarters.

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Pakistan reached an agreement with the International Monetary Fund that could unlock another $1.2 billion in financing, offering fresh support to an economy grappling with elevated inflation and the fallout from the Middle East conflict.

The deal, a staff-level agreement which still needs approval from the IMF’s Executive Board, would give Pakistan about $1 billion under its main lending program and another $210 million under a separate climate fund. That would bring total payouts under the two programs to about $5.7 billion.

The IMF said Pakistan had managed to preserve economic stability despite higher energy prices and supply disruptions stemming from the Middle East conflict. It estimated the economy grew 3.6% in the fiscal year 2026, while foreign-exchange reserves rose to about $21.5 billion by the end of September.

READ: Pakistan Forex Reserves at Record $21.4 Billion on Bond Sale (1)

Show Full Article

The agreement reflects Pakistan’s improving economic outlook and progress on reforms despite its exposure to the conflict. The additional funding would give Islamabad another buffer to build its foreign-exchange reserves and sustain its recovery after years of economic turmoil.

Pakistan is particularly exposed to the turmoil because much of its energy imports passes through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that carries oil and gas from Gulf producers to global markets.

The IMF said headline inflation, after peaking in May, moderated to about 10.3% percent in September, while core inflation remained contained. It said the State Bank of Pakistan should maintain an appropriately tight policy stance to ensure inflation returns durably to the central bank’s target range.

Wildlife populations dropped by an average of 73% across globe from 1970 to 2022, says WWF

The steepest average population declines were in South America, at 95%. It was 80% for Africa in the same 52-year period.

Reuters

08 October, 2026 12:17 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

FILE PHOTO: A giraffe and zebras walk at a water point at the Amboseli National Park as authorities investigate the deaths of 18 elephants in Kenya's Amboseli ecosystem, in Kajiado County, Kenya, August 26, 2026. REUTERS/Monicah Mwangi/File Photo

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Singapore: Nearly 6,000 monitored vertebrate species across more than 35,000 populations declined by an average of 73% from 1970 to 2022, the World Wide Fund for Nature said in its latest Living Planet Report published on Thursday.

* The Living Planet Index, managed by the Zoological Society of London and WWF, monitored a total of 35,803 populations covering 5,790 different species of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish over the 52-year period.

* The 2026 Living Planet Report estimates that overall populations fell by an average of around 2.5% per year over the period.

Show Full Article

• “Monitored global populations continue to decline on average with no evidence yet of that global recovery,” said Andrew Terry, chief conservation officer at ZSL.

* The average rate of decline across the monitored populations does not represent a headcount of the total number of animals lost from 1970 to 2022, and the number is especially sensitive to changes in already small populations.

* Monitored freshwater species saw an average decline of 85%, while terrestrial species fell 69% and marine species 59%, the index showed.

* The steepest average population declines were in South America, at 95%, with Africa also experiencing losses of 80% from 1970 to 2022.

• The 2026 Living Planet report incorporated an additional 295 species and 967 populations across a longer time series compared to the last report in 2024.

* The additional data “reinforces our confidence in the continued decline in biodiversity,” Terry told a briefing.

* Habitat loss and degradation were the most frequently reported threat, but wildlife populations are also at risk from overexploitation, climate change, pollution, invasive species and disease, the report said.

* “Amid these steep declines, there are grounds for hope, rooted in evidence. Wildlife populations are under pressure but recovery is in reach,” said Kirsten Schuijt, WWF’s director general.

* Targeted conservation efforts have enabled populations of some species to recover, including tigers, Atlantic and Pacific bluefin tuna, southern African elephants and green sea turtles.

* Alongside conservation efforts, changes in the energy, food and finance systems are required to halt nature loss, Schuijt said.

(Reporting by David Stanway; Editing by Kate Mayberry)

Pakistan has 48% of the poor in Greater Middle East; poverty in region remains at pre-pandemic levels

World Bank report says the region accounts for 14% of the world’s extreme poor, second only to Sub-Saharan Africa. The increase was driven by rise in poverty in Pakistan.

Debdutta Chakraborty

08 October, 2026 12:07 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational image | Akhtar Soomro | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Pakistan is home to nearly half of the people living on less than $3 a day across the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (MENAAP) region, the World Bank’s Economic Update on the region said Tuesday.

Pakistan accounts for 48 percent of the overall poverty in the region, the report says. This drove the regional increase, which is why MENAAP is the only world region where poverty remains above pre-pandemic levels and is still rising.

Three dollars is 830 Pakistani rupees and Rs 290. Pakistan’s poverty rate rose 6.4 percentage points at the $3.00 line and 3.2 points at the $4.20 line between 2018-19 and 2024-25 and exceeded 20 percent. Poverty rate is the ratio of the population whose income falls below the poverty line.

Show Full Article

Afghanistan, Syria and Yemen accounted for another 47 percent of the region’s population living below the same poverty threshold, according to the report .

Earlier in February, poverty in Pakistan surged to an 11-year high of 29 percent, while income inequality has reached its highest level in 27 years, according to the country’s official statistics.

The World Bank said the region accounted for 14 percent of the world’s extreme poor, second only to Sub-Saharan Africa.

“The increase was driven primarily by a rise in poverty in Pakistan,” the report said, noting that the country’s poverty rate increased by 6.4 percentage points at the $3-a-day line and by 3.2 percentage points at the $4.20 line between 2018-19 and 2024-25.

The bank attributed the deterioration to the Covid-19 pandemic, the devastating 2022 floods, a macroeconomic crisis characterised by high inflation and currency depreciation, and a prolonged period of economic adjustment that weakened real household incomes and employment opportunities.

The latest estimates show that poverty at the $3-a-day threshold has approached or exceeded 20 percent in Djibouti, Pakistan, Syria and Yemen.

The World Bank then projected Pakistan’s economy to grow 3.8 percent in the current fiscal year, while inflation is expected to reach 8.2 percent. However, once population growth is taken into account, real GDP per capita is projected to rise by only 2.2 percent, compared with 2.1 percent last year.

Also Read: Indians live 2.8 years longer than Pakistanis, says WHO. Here’s why

Shifts through the years The 2024 World Bank update had projected 2.8 percent growth in FY25, 3.2 per cent in FY26, and inflation easing to 9 percent in FY26 for Pakistan and a current account deficit forecast at 0.7 percent of GDP in FY26. For 2025, the MENAAP report put Pakistan’s FY2025-26 growth at 2.6 percent and FY2026-27 at 3.4 percent. The bank has forecast a current account deficit of 0.8 percent of GDP and a fiscal deficit of 3.5 percent this fiscal year. Both are higher than the previous year, but remain within what the report described as manageable levels.

In 2025 the main threat was floods and weak agriculture. In 2026 it is the Gulf conflict, with fuel price jumps, a weaker current account, possible remittance losses, and El Niño exposure.

The World Bank said governments across the region were facing competing demands to protect households from rising prices while also responding to humanitarian needs arising from regional conflicts.

Fuel prices have risen sharply since the start of the West Asia conflict. Petrol prices increased by 40 per cent or more in Lebanon, Pakistan, Syria and the United Arab Emirates, while diesel prices rose by more than 40 per cent in Pakistan and the West Bank and Gaza.

According to the report, Pakistan sits in the “developing oil importers” group, which is projected to grow 4.3 percent in 2026, while the Gulf economies contract sharply.

Moreover, poorer households spend 35–50 percent of their budgets on food, so higher food and fuel prices hit them hardest. Pakistan is also among the countries where gasoline prices rose 40 percent or more, and diesel is up over 40 percent since the conflict began.

The increases were substantially higher in some other countries, with diesel prices rising by more than 80 percent in Lebanon and nearly 70 percent in the UAE.

Pakistan remains particularly vulnerable as an oil-importing economy. Along with Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Morocco and Tunisia, it faces the risk of higher inflation and commodity prices, reduced fiscal space, weaker remittance flows from Gulf economies and higher borrowing costs as geopolitical risks persist.

Pakistan’s inflation reached about 11 percent by midyear, according to the report. The fiscal-year forecast of 7.1 percent is however lower than the previous year, and the report projects it rising further to 8.2 percent in FY2027.

In fiscal and external position, Pakistan slips from a surplus to a growing deficit and is listed among the economies facing “significant debt or financing pressures”, alongside Algeria, Djibouti, Iraq, and Morocco.

The report notes that to counter it the government has introduced targeted fuel and farm assistance as it advocates for targeted cash transfers over broad subsidies as cheaper and better for fiscal space.

Then there are remittances. Pakistan is a major labour-sending economy to the Gulf. A prolonged slowdown in Gulf tourism, construction, and hospitality could weaken the income flowing home and remittance decline is named as a risk channel for oil importers generally.

The World Bank reclassified Pakistan, along with Afghanistan, from its South Asia region into a newly created grouping known as MENAAP — Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan in 2025.

Pakistan’s economic and external debt profile increasingly resembled that of MENA economies. Its debt-to-GDP ratio, estimated at around 33.4 percent, is broadly comparable with regional patterns in the region.

Pakistan also shares several demographic and labour-market characteristics with MENA countries, including a high youth dependency ratio, low employment-to-population rates and relatively weak labour-force participation. Female participation in the workforce remains particularly low, mirroring a broader challenge across much of the region.

Pakistan’s economic fortunes are increasingly connected to the Gulf and wider west Asia through remittances, capital flows and energy dependence. These ties have become an important component of Pakistan’s macroeconomic stability, outweighing the country’s relatively limited economic integration with other South Asian economies.

This is an updated version of the report.

(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

Hegseth’s Pentagon purge goes beyond generals. It’s a fight over what the US military is

Generals have been pushed out, thousands of Pentagon jobs cut and old policies scrapped. What is Hegseth trying to build?

Raunaq Lekhi

08 October, 2026 11:18 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Hegseth has removed or forced the early retirement of a string of senior officers (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

As Donald Trump remakes American power in his second term, Pete Hegseth has been carrying out a parallel upheaval inside the Pentagon. While the president has pushed a more muscular “America First” foreign policy, challenged old alliances, pursued US interests in Greenland and repeatedly sought to redraw the boundaries of what American power can do, his defence secretary has been busy reshaping the institution that is supposed to deliver that power.

Hegseth’s mission has been described in sharply different terms depending on who is describing it. He calls it accountability, reform and a return to the “warrior ethos”. His supporters see a long-overdue attack on an enormous bureaucracy that has become too slow, too expensive and too detached from the battlefield. His critics call it a purge, a political takeover of the military or even a threat to the professional officer corps. Hegseth himself has described his fight with the Pentagon bureaucracy as a “war of attrition”.

For defence ministries around the world, particularly those struggling with bloated headquarters and slow procurement, there is a lesson here whichever side they take: what to copy, and what not to do.

Show Full Article

So, is there a method behind Hegseth’s apparent madness?

What has Hegseth actually done? Hegseth has fired, forced out or accelerated the departure of more than a dozen senior military leaders since taking charge of the Pentagon, an unusually large turnover at the top of the US armed forces. The departures have included Gen. Charles “CQ” Brown Jr., then chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; Adm. Lisa Franchetti, the Navy’s first woman chief of naval operations; Adm. Linda Fagan, the Coast Guard commandant; Gen. James Slife, the Air Force vice chief; and later Army chief of staff Gen. Randy George. Other senior commanders, including Gen. Chris Donahue, have also left earlier than expected. In several cases, the Pentagon has not publicly given detailed reasons for the departures.

Then Hegseth went beyond individual firings.

In September, he announced that the US military would cut 20% of its general and flag officer positions by 1 January 2027, doubling an earlier 10% reduction. That affects roughly 800 positions across the services. Hegseth argues that the military has too many senior officers and headquarters layers for the size of the force.

The symbolism is deliberate. Hegseth has repeatedly contrasted “generals” and “G.I.s”, arguing that the Pentagon should have fewer people at the top and more resources reaching those who actually fight.

But the cuts have not been restricted to men and women in uniform.

The Pentagon’s civilian workforce fell from more than 793,000 employees in January 2025 to 714,780 a year later, a reduction of about 10%. The Pentagon approved roughly 53,200 deferred resignations, while a hiring freeze also sharply reduced recruitment.

That is where one of the strongest arguments for Hegseth’s approach and one of the strongest arguments against it collide.

The Pentagon really is a vast bureaucracy. But the Government Accountability Office found that the department did not consistently assess the effects of the 2025 civilian cuts on workload, readiness and other functions. Officials also reported both benefits from organisational streamlining and problems caused by reduced capacity.

The less obvious part of the purge Hegseth’s project is not simply about reducing headcount.

He has also tried to change what the US military considers important.

The Pentagon dismantled its diversity, equity and inclusion infrastructure, changed policies concerning transgender service members and pushed for sex-neutral physical standards for combat jobs. Hegseth has argued that the military should select people according to whether they can meet the requirements of the job, rather than demographic targets.

He has also targeted what he sees as an overly permissive military culture, including grooming standards and physical fitness.

Some of these measures are popular with conservative veterans and Trump’s political base. Others have been attacked as culture-war politics being imported into an institution that traditionally tries to keep partisan battles outside the chain of command.

Hegseth’s September speech at Quantico made that political character difficult to ignore. He attacked what he called the Pentagon’s previous “woke” culture and accused some senior officers of treating civilian control of the military as a “suggestion”.

He also created an Office of Religious Affairs reporting directly to him. The Pentagon says it will strengthen religious support and the military chaplaincy. Critics fear it could give evangelical Christianity disproportionate influence inside a military that includes people of many faiths and those with no religion.

But there is a serious strategy underneath it This is the part that can get lost when Hegseth is reduced to the culture-war headlines.

Some of his objectives are hardly radical.

The US military does have an enormous bureaucracy. Its procurement system is famously slow. Its weapons can cost extraordinary amounts of money and take years to develop. And the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have demonstrated how quickly drones, artificial intelligence, cheap autonomous systems and electronic warfare are changing the battlefield.

Hegseth wants the Pentagon to adapt to that reality.

His most striking move came in September, when he announced the creation of Autowarcom, a new four-star command focused on autonomous warfare, including drones and artificial intelligence. The Pentagon is also working on a broader review of future warfare involving Elon Musk, defence entrepreneur Palmer Luckey and former Republican House speaker Newt Gingrich.

The logic is straightforward: instead of relying predominantly on small numbers of extraordinarily expensive platforms, the US should also be able to produce large numbers of cheaper, intelligent and expendable systems.

That could mean drone swarms replacing some traditional battlefield functions, autonomous systems working alongside soldiers and AI compressing the time between identifying a target and acting on it.

Hegseth is also pushing to strengthen domestic defence supply chains and reduce dependence on vulnerable foreign sources, particularly where China could potentially exert leverage.

In that sense, the Pentagon overhaul is not simply a purge of people. It is also an attempt to change what the Pentagon buys, who it buys it from and how quickly it can put new technology into the hands of troops.

So why the backlash? The biggest concern is not that Hegseth wants reform. It is how he is carrying it out.

The US military depends on a professional officer corps whose job is to give civilian leaders candid advice, including advice they may not want to hear.

Critics argue that repeatedly removing senior commanders without clearly explaining the reasons can create a different incentive: officers may become more cautious about disagreeing with political leadership.

Sen. Jack Reed, the senior Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, has repeatedly accused Hegseth of politicising the military. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis has gone further. In a forthcoming memoir, Tillis called his vote to confirm Hegseth his “biggest regret” and criticised the secretary’s management style.

That makes the opposition unusual. Hegseth is not facing criticism only from Democrats or the traditional defence establishment. Some Republicans who supported his appointment are now questioning where the overhaul is going.

There is also concern about what happens when institutional knowledge disappears faster than it can be replaced.

A military headquarters may be bloated. But not every person working inside it is redundant. Civilian employees maintain weapons programmes, logistics, intelligence, contracts, bases and medical systems. The GAO has already identified cases where civilian reductions created staffing problems at remote military installations.

And then there is the media fight Hegseth’s relationship with the press has been unusually hostile for a Pentagon chief.

His department imposed new restrictions on journalists covering the Pentagon, including rules governing access and the gathering of information. Major organisations including The New York Times, Washington Post, AP, Reuters, NPR and Fox News rejected the new arrangements rather than accept restrictions they considered incompatible with independent reporting.

Hegseth has repeatedly attacked journalists who publish stories critical of his management of the Pentagon or the Trump administration’s wars. At his latest Quantico address, he devoted part of his speech to attacking what he called “anti-American losers” in the news media.

Supporters see this as Hegseth refusing to let Washington’s traditional defence press dictate the agenda.

Critics see it as a serious problem for democratic oversight: if the Pentagon becomes harder for independent journalists to penetrate, Congress and the public have fewer ways of knowing what is happening inside it.

Who is actually with Hegseth? Trump, above all.

The president has given Hegseth considerable freedom to reshape the Pentagon and shares his distrust of what both men describe as an entrenched Washington establishment.

Hegseth also has support among conservative veterans, military commentators and online personalities who believe the US armed forces became too bureaucratic and too focused on issues such as DEI rather than combat readiness.

The Pentagon has increasingly drawn figures from that conservative military-media ecosystem into government roles, blurring the old distinction between military commentary and military policymaking. That has alarmed some traditionalists, who fear that the officer corps is being divided along political lines.

But there is a less ideological constituency for some of Hegseth’s reforms too: defence technologists and people inside the military who have long complained that the Pentagon struggles to adopt commercial technology quickly enough.

The drone and AI push therefore has supporters who have little interest in the culture war.

What is at stake? The real test of Hegseth’s Pentagon will not be whether he can fire generals.

It will be whether he can replace an old system with a better one.

If cutting headquarters layers frees money and talented people for weapons, training and frontline units, Hegseth could eventually be credited with doing something previous defence secretaries talked about but failed to accomplish.

If faster procurement gets useful drones and AI systems into the hands of soldiers years earlier than conventional programmes would have, his argument will look stronger still.

But if experienced officers leave faster than new leadership can be developed, civilian cuts weaken essential functions, promotions become associated with political loyalty and independent scrutiny becomes harder, the Pentagon could emerge smaller but not necessarily stronger.

That is why armies around the world are watching.

Every major military has the same basic problem Hegseth has identified: large defence bureaucracies accumulate layers, programmes and habits that are difficult to remove.

The American experiment is now testing two very different propositions at once.

The first is that a powerful military can become more effective by cutting deeply into its hierarchy and bureaucracy.

The second is that this can be done without damaging the professional institutions, expertise and dissent that made that military powerful in the first place.

Hegseth believes both can be achieved.

His critics think he may prove the first point by breaking the second.

That is the real wager behind the Pentagon purge.
